means either digging through your telemetry or pasting a stack trace into an LLM that can’t see what actually happened.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Sentry already has that context -- every error, trace, log, replay, and profile from your application. Seer is the AI layer that reasons over all of it to automate debugging.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Next time something’s not quite right, describe what you’re seeing and Seer Agent investigates across your full telemetry to tell you what’s going on and why.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Click ‘Ask Seer’ in Sentry to try it, or mention @Sentry in Slack to start debugging.</p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/Sentry_050426","text":"Try Sentry's Seer Agent","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/b8aeab84-dcff-4ca0-8c3b-df72192b6a80?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Try Sentry's Seer Agent</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">LLMs can search the web, pull up your calendar, book reservations, and send emails on your behalf. From the user’s perspective, it seems like typing a request, and the thing just happens.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">There is, however, a lot happening underneath to make this work.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The model needs to know which tools are available, how to request them, and what to do with the results. The software surrounding the model needs to figure out what it actually wants, execute it safely, and feed the answer back.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Getting all of this right took several iterations, a couple of failed experiments, and eventually an open protocol that every major AI company is now adopting.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In this article, we will look at this progression that has happened from basic tool use to function calling to the Model Context Protocol, allowing the LLMs to go from isolated text generation tools to assistants that can do interesting stuff for the end users.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Why LLMs Cannot Act on Their Own</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">To understand why connecting LLMs to external systems is an interesting engineering problem, it helps to understand what an LLM actually does.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">At their core, large language models are text-prediction engines. They take text in and produce text out. They are extraordinarily good at this. In fact, so good that the output often looks like real reasoning, but the underlying mechanism is always the same: predict the next token based on everything that came before.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This means an LLM has no built-in ability to call an API, query a database, or perform any action in the real world. Ask it “What’s the weather in Tokyo right now?” and it can give a plausible-sounding answer based on patterns in its training data, but it cannot actually check. It has no network access. It has no way to reach outside the boundaries of its own context window, the finite amount of text it can consider at once.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/e99aecf5-a33a-4a29-9ad8-49fd563df4cc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/1df71e21-5907-42aa-8eac-313641100529_2450x1228.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":730,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":111102,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/196046262?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1df71e21-5907-42aa-8eac-313641100529_2450x1228.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This is a direct result of what the technology is at its core. But it creates an obvious question: if LLMs can only generate text, how do applications like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini end up doing things like searching the web, sending emails, or pulling data from internal systems?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The answer is that the LLM itself doesn’t perform those actions directly. Each of these products has an application layer, the surrounding software infrastructure, built around the model. That layer lets the model request actions. When ChatGPT searches the web, the model generates a structured request saying “search for X,” and OpenAI’s application infrastructure carries out the actual search and returns the results. The same pattern holds for Claude, Gemini, and any other AI assistant with tool access.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In short, the model reasons about what needs to happen, and the surrounding software makes it happen.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">How Tool Use and Function Calling Work</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">When an LLM-powered application supports tool use, the model receives a menu of available functions alongside each user prompt.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Each function is described with a name, a purpose, and the parameters it accepts, typically defined as a JSON schema (a structured format that specifies what inputs the function expects and what types they should be). When the model encounters a question it cannot answer from its training data alone, it can respond not with a final answer, but with a structured request asking for a specific function to be called with specific arguments.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Here are the steps:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The model generates this request as structured text, usually JSON. It does not execute the function itself.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The application layer receives that structured output, validates it, and actually runs the function (hits a weather API, queries a database, sends an email).</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">It sends the result back to the model as a new message.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The model then uses that result to compose its final response to the user.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">For example, a user asks the application, “What’s the weather in Tokyo?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The model has a tool called get_weather available, which accepts a location parameter. Rather than guessing, the model generates something like {”function”: “get_weather”, “arguments”: {”location”: “Tokyo”}}.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The application layer receives this, calls a real weather API, gets back “22°C, partly cloudy,” and sends that data to the model. The model then responds with a natural language answer grounded in real-time data.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This back-and-forth is called the agentic loop, as shown in the diagram below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure loop can also run for multiple rounds, with the model calling several tools in sequence to fulfill a single request. For example, a user saying “find me flights to Tokyo and check the weather there” might trigger a flight search tool call first, then a weather tool call, with the model synthesizing both results into a single response. This multi-step looping is the foundation of AI agents that are systems where the model autonomously plans and executes complex tasks.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The separation between the model deciding what should happen and the application layer actually doing it has some advantages. The application can restrict which functions the model has access to, validate arguments before executing anything, and require human approval for high-stakes actions like transferring money or deleting data.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This mechanism, formalized as “function calling” or “tool calling,” became widely available in mid-2023 when OpenAI added it as a first-class API feature.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Just a few months earlier, OpenAI had launched ChatGPT Plugins, which let third-party developers expose arbitrary APIs to ChatGPT. However, discovery was difficult, plugin quality varied wildly, and the security model was not mature enough to handle untrusted third-party tools interacting with a language model. OpenAI deprecated plugins entirely by April 2024, moving to the more controlled function-calling approach where developers explicitly define the tools the model can use.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the timeline of evolution as below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: justify">Function calling worked, but it introduced a new problem. Every LLM provider implemented it differently. OpenAI had one schema format, Anthropic had another, and Google had its own. A tool built for one provider’s API wouldn’t work with another without rewriting the integration code. For developers who wanted their tools to work across multiple LLMs, or who wanted flexibility to switch providers, this fragmentation was a genuine obstacle.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">The Model Context Protocol (MCP)</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The fragmentation problem gets worse as the ecosystem grows.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">For example, iff there are 3 LLM providers and 5 tools to integrate, there are 15 possible custom integrations, one for each provider-tool combination. Add a sixth tool, and 3 more integrations are needed. Add a fourth provider and 5 more. The total grows as the product of providers times tools. This is called the N×M problem, and it becomes unmanageable quickly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The Model Context Protocol was designed to solve exactly this.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Introduced by Anthropic as an open standard, MCP defines a common protocol that both LLM applications and tool providers can implement once. Each LLM client implements MCP once. Each tool server implements MCP once. The total number of integrations drops from N×M to N+M. Three providers plus five tools equals 8 implementations instead of 15.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure works through a client-server architecture with three components.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">An MCP Host is the AI application a user interacts with, something like Claude Desktop or an AI-powered IDE.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Inside the host lives an MCP Client, which handles communication with external tool providers.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">On the other side, MCP Servers are lightweight programs that wrap around existing tools, databases, or APIs and expose them in MCP’s standard format.</p></li></ul><div the host starts up, its client connects to available MCP servers and asks each one to describe its capabilities. Those descriptions get fed to the model, and from there, the familiar function calling mechanism takes over.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The model sees the available tools, generates structured requests when it needs them, and the MCP infrastructure routes each request to the right server and returns the result.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Beyond tools, MCP servers can also surface resources (data the model can read, like files or database records) and prompt templates, though tools remain the core capability driving most adoption today.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below that shows a typical request flow using MCP:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px does not replace function calling. Function calling is the mechanism by which the model signals it wants to use a tool. MCP standardizes how those tools are described, discovered, and invoked so that the same tool works with any model that speaks the protocol.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In other words, they are complementary layers solving different parts of the same problem. The model doesn’t know or care whether MCP is involved behind the scenes. It sees a list of tool definitions and generates calls against them, the same way it always has.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Adoption has been remarkably fast.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In 2025, OpenAI announced MCP support across its products. Google DeepMind confirmed support for Gemini shortly after. By late 2025, over 10,000 publicly available MCP servers were listed in online directories. At the end of 2025, Anthropic donated the protocol to the newly formed Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, co-founded by Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI, with support from AWS, Google, Microsoft, Cloudflare, and Bloomberg. What started as an open-source experiment became an industry standard in roughly a year.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">The Costs and Tradeoffs of Tool Use</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">That rapid growth, however, has surfaced real costs and risks that are important to understand.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The most significant is security. Every tool exposed to an LLM expands the system’s attack surface. In September 2025, this became concrete. A developer published an npm package that looked like an official email integration for MCP, mimicking the name and structure of a legitimate library from Postmark, a well-known email service. Hundreds of developers installed it. Later, it was found that a hidden code in the package was silently forwarding copies of every outgoing email to the attacker. This was a supply chain attack, where malicious code is hidden inside a dependency that looks trustworthy, and it was described as the first such attack targeting MCP servers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Security challenges go beyond individual attacks. The protocol initially prioritized ease of adoption over robust security, and the authentication specifications went through multiple revisions as the community worked to close gaps. This is a familiar pattern in technology standards: interoperability and adoption come first, and security matures with time. The MCP specification continues to evolve, with recent revisions addressing authentication, server identity, and governance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Beyond security, there is a subtler cost. Every tool definition exposed to the model consumes tokens in the context window. The name, description, and parameter schema of each tool all occupy space in the same finite context that holds the conversation history and task instructions. A handful of tools creates negligible overhead. Dozens or hundreds start crowding out the room the model needs to reason about the task. An agent with access to hundreds of tools sounds powerful in theory, but in practice, each additional tool slightly degrades the model’s ability to focus on the actual problem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Tool use also does not make LLMs deterministic. The model can still hallucinate function names, pass malformed arguments, or chain tools in unexpected ways. Validation, error handling, and human approval steps are essential parts of any production system that gives an LLM access to real-world capabilities.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">LLMs started as isolated text predictors, powerful but unable to interact with external systems.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Function calling gave them a structured way to request actions while keeping execution in the hands of the surrounding application. MCP standardized how tools are described and discovered, so that integrations work across providers without custom code for every combination.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Through all of these layers, however, one principle remains constant. The model reasons about what should happen, and the application layer controls whether it actually does. That boundary is where security, reliability, and control are designed in.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The space is moving fast. MCP went from launch to industry-wide standard in roughly a year. But the core concepts covered here, tool definitions, the agentic loop, the separation of reasoning from execution, and the tradeoffs that come with expanding what an LLM can reach, are ideas that will transfer regardless of which framework, provider, or protocol version ends up being used.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: item.title: High performance Git
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
High performance Git

a few hours by Ted Nyman Git is more than version control. It's also a database, a cache, a graph walker, and a transfer protocol. Ted's book covers all those layers and what they cost in performance, from objects and history to packfiles, cloning, and transport. It's aimed at engineers who need Git to stay fast as repos and teams grow.
item.description: High performance Git

item.title: How the does Shazam work?
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How the does Shazam work?

Shri Khalpada

8 minutes by Shri Khalpada Shazam ignores melody and lyrics entirely. Instead, it converts sound into a visual map of frequencies, then keeps only the loudest peaks, like a connect the dots picture of the song. Pairs of those peaks generate short codes that act as a fingerprint. Your phone sends those codes to a server, which finds a match across millions of songs in milliseconds by looking up each code directly rather than scanning every song one by one.
item.description: How the does Shazam work?

item.title: You can beat the binary search
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
You can beat the binary search

Daniel Lemire

7 minutes by Daniel Lemire Binary search beats linear search for large sorted arrays, but modern hardware can do even better. By splitting search ranges into quarters instead of halves and using CPU instructions that compare 16 values at once, a new approach called SIMD Quad cuts search times in half or more compared to binary search.
item.description: You can beat the binary search

item.title: The 20 software engineering laws
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The 20 software engineering laws

Milan Milanović

25 minutes by Milan Milanović Software engineering has a set of timeless laws that explain why projects fail, teams slow down, and plans drift. These laws, some over 60 years old, are really about human nature, not technology. Adding people to late projects makes them later, work expands to fill available time, and any metric that becomes a target stops being useful. Learning these laws before a project goes wrong is far cheaper than learning them after.
item.description: The 20 software engineering laws

item.title: An AI agent just destroyed our production data
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
An AI agent just destroyed our production data

Jer Crane

10 minutes by Jer Crane An AI coding agent deleted a small business's production database and all backups with a single API call, wiping three months of customer data. The agent later admitted in writing that it broke every safety rule it had been given. Two vendors share the blame: Cursor's safety guardrails failed to stop the agent, and Railway had no confirmation step for destructive actions, no scoped API tokens, and stored backups inside the same volume they were meant to protect. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: An AI agent just destroyed our production data

item.title: High-performance distributed caching with .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
High-performance distributed caching with .NET

Jared Meade

Jared's guide walks through building a .NET console app with a two-layer caching setup using HybridCache and PostgreSQL. Slow external data calls that take seconds are replaced with responses returning in under a millisecond from memory, or in a fraction of a second from the database cache. When the in-memory cache expires, the database cache keeps things fast, and only after both expire does the app fetch fresh data from the source.
item.description: High-performance distributed caching with .NET

item.title: external APIs
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
external APIs

Adrian Bailador

Adrian explains the Anti-Corruption Layer pattern in .NET, which protects your domain from being polluted by external APIs. He shows how to isolate and translate external models into your own domain language, keeping business logic clean. By using an Anti-Corruption Layer, changes in external systems only affect one layer, making your application easier to maintain, understand, and extend.
item.description: external APIs

item.title: Explore union types in C# 15
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Explore union types in C# 15

Bill Wagner

C# 15 adds union types, letting you declare a value as exactly one of a fixed set of types. The compiler enforces exhaustive pattern matching, so missing cases cause warnings at build time rather than failures at runtime. Types in a union do not need to share a common ancestor. The feature is available now in .NET 11 Preview 2 with language version set to preview.
item.description: Explore union types in C# 15

item.title: ASP.NET Core cookie size limits in production: Causes and fixes
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
ASP.NET Core cookie size limits in production: Causes and fixes

Khalid Abuhakmeh

Khalid argues that authentication can fail in production due to oversized cookies. ASP.NET Core stores user claims in cookies, which can grow too large from many claims, tokens, or multiple schemes. This causes silent login failures or HTTP 431 errors. Solutions include reducing claims, disabling token storage, clearing old cookies, or using server-side sessions. The best approach is minimizing cookie data and loading user information on demand.
item.description: ASP.NET Core cookie size limits in production: Causes and fixes

item.title: Build your own CQRS dispatcher in .NET 10
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Build your own CQRS dispatcher in .NET 10

Mukesh Murugan

MediatR went commercial in July 2025, pushing many teams to find alternatives. In this article, Mukesh built a custom CQRS dispatcher in .NET 10 that replaces MediatR with about 100 lines of code, supports the same pipeline behavior pattern, returns ValueTask for fewer allocations, and benchmarks 4.4x faster than MediatR 12.4.1 on real BenchmarkDotNet runs. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Build your own CQRS dispatcher in .NET 10

Skills run in the agent's own environment with no extra infra.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Where it fits: Use MCP to connect agents to live systems and data. families: model-level and system-level.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Model-level defenses teach the model to resist injection.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Spotlighting wraps untrusted text in control tags like <UNTRUSTED>...</UNTRUSTED> and tells the model to treat anything inside as data, not instructions.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Instruction Hierarchy fine-tunes the model to rank the developer's system prompt above the user's message, and both above third-party content.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">System-level defenses build a system around the LLM that bounds the damage.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Least-Privilege Tools: Give the agent the minimum tools it needs.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Human-in-the-Loop: Require explicit user approval before any sensitive action runs.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Planner / Executor Split: Two separate LLMs. The planner has tool access but never sees untrusted content. The executor reads untrusted content but has no tools.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">No single defense is enough. Production systems like Gmail stack them, and together they make indirect injection manageable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Over to you: what's the one defense you've seen work in production that isn't on this list?</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Next, it gathers candidate posts from two sources: Thunder (posts from accounts you follow) and Phoenix Retrieval (posts from 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">These candidates get enriched with metadata like author info and media details during Hydration, then pass through Filtering, which removes duplicates, old posts, blocked authors, and muted keywords.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: item.title: How To Be Direct And Strategic
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Be Direct And Strategic

Yue Zhao

"I saw an issue with a process on my team recently and brought it up directly in a team meeting a few days later. I was very direct about the problem, gave all the details, and explained how it impacted everyone. To my surprise, my manager shut it down completely, and now I cannot get any buy-in from anyone. What happened? Where did I do wrong?"

#Leadership Communication
item.description: How To Be Direct And Strategic

item.title: Speak In The Affirmative: "Do This" Versus "Don't Do That"
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Speak In The Affirmative: "Do This" Versus "Don't Do That"

Wes Kao

“It’s to your benefit to be as clear as possible when you speak or write, because clear communication helps you get what you need. One way to do this is to speak in the affirmative, rather than the negative... If you speak in negatives, your recipient has to take an extra mental step.”

#Leadership Management Communication
item.description: Speak In The Affirmative: "Do This" Versus "Don't Do That"

item.title: How I Use AI To Code
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How I Use AI To Code

Chris Parsons

A practitioner's guide to AI-assisted coding in 2026. Senior engineers should shift from reviewing AI-generated diffs to training the harness that produces them via CLAUDE.md files, skill files, and feedback loops. The bottleneck has moved from code generation to verification.

#AI Guide BestPractices
item.description: How I Use AI To Code

item.title: Structured-Prompt-Driven Development
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Structured-Prompt-Driven Development

“Instead of relying on ad hoc chats, SPDD turns prompts into assets that can be: version controlled, reviewed, reused, and improved over time. Teams use structured prompts to capture requirements, domain language, design intent, constraints, and a task breakdown. Then the LLM generates code within a defined boundary, so output becomes more predictable and easier to validate.”

#AI Guide BestPractices
item.description: Structured-Prompt-Driven Development

item.title: Email Is Crazy
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Email Is Crazy

Saurabh Khawase

“Email evolved organically over the years, tracing its origins to the academic labs of ARPANET in the ’70s. Its various components were designed by different people, at different times, facing different challenges. The email ecosystem is a very complex beast with more than 100 RFCs mandating its various protocols.” A deep dive into how email works under the hood.

#Infrastructure DeepDive
item.description: Email Is Crazy

item.title: How To Make A Fast Dynamic Language Interpreter
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Make A Fast Dynamic Language Interpreter

Fil Pizlo

“This post is about optimizing an extremely simple AST-walking interpreter for a dynamic language called Zef that I created for fun to the point where it is competitive with the likes of Lua, QuickJS, and CPython.”

#SystemDesign DeepDive

20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;text-align: justify">Think about the difference between leaving a housemate a to-do list and writing them a contract. The to-do list says “buy bread on Monday, take out the bins Tuesday, water the plants Wednesday.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">It’s a sequence of instructions, and if any step fails or gets skipped, the whole thing fails. The contract says something different. It says the kitchen should always have bread, the bins should never overflow, and the plants should never go three days without water. One is a script. The other is a promise, and somebody has to keep checking whether the promise is being kept.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Kubernetes is what we get when that second approach is taken seriously and built into a whole infrastructure platform.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In this article, we will learn how Kubernetes is a system of promises, and that every piece of it is a small program keeping one of those promises.</p><div style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em><span>Hi, this is Gergely with a bonus, free issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover Big Tech and startups through the lens of senior engineers and engineering leaders. Today, we cover one out of three topics from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/17d55837-434a-4828-993a-197c8eb3a4f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">last week’s The Pulse</a><span> issue. Full subscribers received the article below seven days ago. If you’ve been forwarded this email, you can</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8fb53e4d-9f43-4902-af34-56360e0ba368?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"> subscribe here</a><span>.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Last week, we covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d75f15f8-53fa-412e-9807-c6643dfa872a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">the slightly perverse trend of “tokenmaxxing”</a><span> across the industry, where devs run agents with the sole aim of boosting their personal “token stats” in an effort to rank higher on internal token leaderboards, and not be seen as a Luddite who doesn’t use AI tools enough compared to peers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This week, I spoke with a software engineer at a large company and another at a seed-stage place. Both shared almost identical stories: at their latest all-hands, company leadership expressed concerns about the fast-rising costs of tokens. At both places, token spend has increased by ~10x in the last six months – with no signs of slowing down.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I wanted to find out about this trend, so I talked to devs at 15 businesses. Below is what I learned about what’s happening in workplaces of all sizes. Names are anonymized.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">Large companies</h2><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Setting the default model to a cheaper one: 10,000+ person SaaS company, offices on all continents</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Inside a large SaaS company, most devs use an internal background coding tool for coding. This model defaults to Claude Sonnet, which is the cheaper Claude version. Model selection is not persisted, so devs who prefer working with Opus, for instance, must reselect it on every subsequent startup.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This tool supports all major frontier models such as Sonnet, Opus, GPT, and Gemini. Devs at the company whom I talked to are very heavy users of the tool and have not encountered usage limitations.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Fintech company, US, Series D, ~8,000 people. Staff engineer:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“The cost in token spend is off the charts – and leadership has shared this trend with us. They have not said anything beyond showing growth in spend, and mentioning that this won’t be sustainable. So, nothing specific yet, but my sense is that something will have to change. Limits or prioritizing cheaper models, cutting back on hiring? Who knows.”</p></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Infra company, US, publicly traded, ~5,000 people. Engineering Director:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>“We’re monitoring but not restricting.</strong><span> We are spot checking the heaviest users, but we are seeing the business cases working out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We are offering some guidance on model selection - e.g., turn off the new high-effort setting in Claude. Some users are trying open source models – but open source model usage is a bottom-up initiative, not a top-down one.”</p></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Information technology, US, 10,000+ people. Director of Engineering:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“We have already had to raise our API budget limits multiple times in April. We recently switched to a much higher-effort level for Claude, which significantly increased the cost per PR.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>One reason for the cost spike is using state-of-the-art models for demanding tasks.</strong><span> We are using that high-effort setting even for fairly trivial tasks that could have been handled by much cheaper models, or even by lower-effort Claude loops. Despite a few of us pointing this out, leadership has basically said budget is not the concern right now.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I sense that the budget increase has not been forecasted, and we’re in for a reckoning.</span><strong> </strong><span>I suspect the attitude changes once finance and other cost-conscious parts of the org realize we are spending hundreds of dollars per day, per highly-engaged developer. For now, fear of missing out and not wanting to fall behind seems to be outweighing cost discipline.”</span></p></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Games studio, US+Europe, ~5,000 people. Senior developer:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“What budget increase? It’s very hard to get a budget for AI here! Claude Code is still not rolled out because $200/month/dev is seen as too high a cost. I talk with people at startups where $1,000/month in spending is totally normal, and it’s night and day here.”</p></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Fintech company, US+Europe, late stage, ~5,000 people. Staff engineer:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>“Some developers are now spending $500 a day (!!) on Claude Code.</strong><span> Practically speaking, this means that employee costs have doubled. Productivity has increased, in my view, but now the bottleneck is code reviews. AI can spit out code quite quickly, but we still have human reviews in place. Leadership encourages using AI for code review, but my team will not blindly trust AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The push from AI is coming from the top. This year’s performance review had a section on AI, rating devs by how well they used AI, so this is another reason everyone just uses it as much as they can.”</p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">Mid-sized companies</h2><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">SaaS industry, US, ~2,000 people. Dev Productivity Lead:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Model routing helped keep our costs growing less dramatically. For example, changing the default model reduced cost by 30%. This is our strategy with AI spend, summarized:</p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Short term: spend, spend, spend!</strong><span> Experiment and use whatever models make sense.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Measure the impact</strong><span>. Measure key outcomes and report on spend, monthly.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>When spend vs results diverge: adjust. </strong><span>When our spend increases dramatically, but outcomes don’t follow: see what we can do to adjust the delta. More spend should mean better outcomes. If not, we are doing something wrong.”</span></p></li></ul></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Finance industry, US, ~2,000 people. VP of AI:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“We have Cursor and Claude Desktop, both of which have around 800-1,200 total users. Token usage is growing somewhat unexpectedly. Estimates are being adjusted on the fly; the initial plan to have strict limits (say, $100 per user) is breaking when reality hits, and people exhaust them in 3-5 working days.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Using expensive models is a problem. In regards to Cursor, many devs are defaulting to the most expensive models without realizing that going with Opus gives single percentage gains in intelligence compared to Sonnet, for example, while exhausting their budgets almost immediately.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>We are working on blocking/managing out the most expensive models [with Cursor]</strong><span>, as going into thousands of dollars per user, per month is not sustainable on our scale. Cursor is a good partner and we’re working with them to switch to a “pooled spend” model where heavy users can tap into a pool of extra spend.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Claude is a similar story. We were at $100 of Claude Desktop limit for everyone, but as we are moving forward, I can see that we would need to go much higher, especially for business-critical use cases.”</p></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Infra company, US, late-stage, ~700 people. Founder:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“We haven’t had much of an issue. Most folks police themselves for runaway costs; for example, we had someone hit like $10K in a week because they messed up caching, but it was caught and they corrected their harness.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>For the most part, we don’t see our high-end folks spending more than ~$1K/week.</strong><span> Now, to be clear, this is not a small amount! BUT it’s already a small subset of the population.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We’re just factoring it into engineering costs at this point: if it’s, say, $2K/month per employee, that’s $24K per year.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Who cares, then, when engineers already cost $200-400K/year in cash comp? Okay, so what if it’s $5K/month. That’s $60K/year.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Our bet is that token costs will stabilize and we’ll eventually end up with local-ish models.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now, it could be five years before they stabilize, but overall, spend today isn’t that insane to me.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s a lot of people who are just dumb about it, but most legit execs push back on this. Take the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3fe5226f-c471-464d-b885-a473ce5635a7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Ralph loops</a><span> or other insanity where someone spends $1K/day, $5K/week or stuff like this. That’s all just people being fools thinking they’re doing “R&D,” or somehow that they’re smarter than everyone else, but they’re just producing junk that never ships or is not useful.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>We saw a bit of “stupid overspend” in the first couple months, but that’s all gone now. </strong><span>Costs could go up even more if we would “crack the whip” in wanting to see even more output, but we’re not doing that.”</span></p></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Healthcare industry, US, ~500 people. Senior engineering manager:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong>We are not holding back on spend, and have a monthly spend leaderboard.</strong><span> And we WANT devs to spend more on tokens! For example, one of my engineers spent $1,400 on a long Claude Code session in a single day.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>We are seeing massive leverage, and we do more with the same number of people. </strong><span>This is why we are okay with our spending spiking. Our traffic is growing more than 10x, year-on-year, and we have managed to keep things running with the same team, and these AI tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Engineering is now blocked on Product and Design – which never happened before! This is how fast execution has become. We now have Staff+ engineers writing Product PRDs so we can move faster.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’ve been in tech for close to 15 years and I never saw dramatic change like this. I just came back after a 3-month break, and every single thing is different in my day! I feel these AI agents are the biggest change in the industry since high-level languages became widespread.”</p></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">E-commerce company, US & Europe, ~2,000 devs. Head of Engineering:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“The increase in spend is INSANE. It’s about usage going up, with no signs of stopping. Usage is off the charts.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We currently do not have limits in place, and are not pausing now. Our CEO is AI-pilled and won’t let us slow down.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>We do buy tokens at a discount. </strong><span>They start from 5% and go up with usage with the vendors we use (the usual suspects.)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We don’t let devs use anything lower than Opus 4.7 for coding. Cheaper models might work better, but a slight error pushed to prod would result in hours of toil.”</p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">Small companies</h2><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Series A, US, ~50 people. Principal Engineer:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“About 15 devs are heavy users of AI and costs are rising very fast. Almost everyone uses Claude and Claude Code. We are considering four potential options:</p><ol style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Increase AI budget, and start measuring more</strong><span>. Continue doing what we are, but allow devs to use more tokens instead of hiring limits. The precise ROI is hard to quantify, but we’ll start to measure and track both AI adoption and impact.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Optimize token consumption. </strong><span>Use cheaper models for simpler tasks, review token usage, and see where we can cut usage. Downside: this approach could become one with diminishing returns, fast.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Integrate more AI providers in the company.</strong><span> Find wrappers to abstract LLMs. The problem is: how do you replace Claude Code, for instance?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Pivot to local models:</strong><span> such as Kimi, Qwen, and so on. The problem is it’s a big investment in high-end hardware or cloud GPUs. Upside: it offers better long-term cost control, once done.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We are likely to go with option #1: increase spend BUT maintain momentum and put the right measurements in place. We can do #2, #3 and #4 later. But if we kill AI usage momentum inside the company, the outcome will probably be worse.”</p></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">AI infra, US, seed stage, ~15 people. Founder:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong>We saw a 15x increase in 6 months:</strong></p><ul style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Six months ago our spend per developer was ~$200/month</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Today, it’s around $3,000/developer/month, for our seven devs</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We’re not slowing usage, especially as we are building an AI infra product. The increase was much faster than expected, though.”</p></blockquote><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.125em;">Small, bootstrapped company, Europe. Founding engineer:</h4><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Our current strategy in dealing with the increase in costs is to switch to a cheaper model; unfortunately, from Opus to Sonnet in our case. That said, Sonnet is quite decent.”</p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;">How businesses manage token spend</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Regardless of company size, there seems to be two strategies for how companies deal with increased spending. A summary:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Strategy #1: “let it rip and start measuring.” </strong><span>Around half of respondents say AI spend is rising dramatically, and they have decided to do nothing about it. They </span><em>want</em><span> devs to use AI as much as it makes sense to, and to help the work as much as possible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, because the cost is rising dramatically, these companies are now starting to measure usage and attempting to measure the impact of their AI tools.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a few companies where the impact seems to be very positive, already. Smaller startups whose business is exploding in numbers of customers, load, and revenue, see that they don’t need to hire more staff because existing engineers can keep supporting the growth with AI tools.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Strategy #2: curb spending.</strong><span> Commonly mentioned cost-saving approaches:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Use cheaper models for simpler tasks</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Set default models to less capable ones</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Set a spending cap and make it hard for engineers to exceed it, or require consent for doing so</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most companies using strategy #1 have briefly considered going with this approach, but threw it away, because they see this approach as optimizing on the wrong thing: cutting costs before the productivity impact of using state-of-the-art tools is even known!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Discounts exist when the spend is in the millions of dollars. </strong><span>I asked several people if they are getting discounts from vendors when buying tokens at scale. There were no exact numbers, but this is what I gathered in aggregate about possible custom agreements:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Cursor: open to discounts above a few million dollars in spend. </strong><span>Companies have negotiated discounts with Cursor after crossing $1M of spending. Some companies negotiated tiered discounts from this level, starting at 5% and going higher as their spend goes up.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Anthropic: no discounts. </strong><span>I talked with companies spending $5M+ per year on Claude which have received no discounts. If Anthropic offers discounts, it will likely be at a much higher tier.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>All discounts are custom, so try to negotiate – it’s free! </strong><span>Pricing discounts are on a per-customer basis, and highly custom. The easiest way to see if a discount is available is to ask the vendors!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>—-</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Read the full issue of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/17d55837-434a-4828-993a-197c8eb3a4f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">last week’s The Pulse</a><span>, or check out </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a7c4de44-793c-4e18-9e6b-f3c21cc2a72b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">this week’s The Pulse</a><span>. This week’s issue covers:</span></em></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Load from AI breaks GitHub – but why not other vendors? </strong><span>GitHub’s reliability is less than one nine, and getting worse. Prolific open source contributor, Mitchell Hashimoto, is quitting GitHub because he thinks it’s not suited for professional work. GitHub’s leadership blames the 3.5x increase in service load as the cause of degradation – or it might be self-inflicted.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Anthropic’s speedrun to destroy trust.</strong><span> Anthropic could do no wrong until recently, but in the past month, that’s all changed. Silently nerfing Claude Code, banning companies from Claude, and baffling price rises all add to a sense that Anthropic is in its “extraction” era of generating more revenue for the same or worse service.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Industry pulse. </strong><span>Dramatic price increases at GitHub Copilot, explosive growth at Codex, Google scrambling to build a good coding model, Cursor might be bought by SpaceX, AI agent deletes car business, and more.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Mitchell Hashimoto & the “building block economy</strong><span>.</span><strong>” </strong><span>Ghostty’s creator finds that open source “building blocks” are the best way to win massive adoption by software components – but it’s got harder to build a business on top of open building blocks.</span></p></li></ol></div></div><div class="container-border" models. Few optimize inference. We benchmarked NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell on Akamai Cloud against H100 using real LLM workloads.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">At 100 concurrent requests, Blackwell reached 24,240 tokens/sec per server, compared to 1,863 TPS on H100. That’s up to 1.63× higher throughput, with additional gains from FP4 precision. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The difference comes down to architecture. These GPUs run on a globally distributed platform built for real-time, latency-sensitive inference, not centralized batch jobs. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you're building agentic systems or high-concurrency AI apps, infrastructure choices matter as much as model selection. See the full setup, methodology, and results. Three years earlier, Wise was deploying with a simpler in-house tool that treated each release as a basic transaction, where the process was essentially to push the code and hope for the best.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This leap was made possible by some interesting engineering decisions that we will learn about in this article.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">For reference, Wise moves about £36 billion across borders every quarter, with 65% of transfers arriving instantly. One might assume that kind of reliability requires a tightly controlled, top-down engineering organization. However, the opposite is true.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Wise has 850+ engineers organized into autonomous squads, each empowered to make their own technical decisions. The reason this works, and the reason it would collapse without a very specific set of infrastructure investments, is the real engineering story behind Wise.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Behind the product that 15.6 million active customers interact with, there are over 1000 microservices, 700+ Java repositories, 40 web applications, and native iOS and Android apps with hundreds of modules each. What holds all of this together is an internal platform, a set of shared tools, frameworks, and automated systems that make the right engineering choice the easy one.</p><div
